name: grep
one_line: print lines that match a pattern
plain: `grep` reads text and prints only the lines that contain what you are looking for. It is how you find a flag, a password, an IP address or an error in a pile of text.
You give it a pattern and one or more files (or pipe text into it). Patterns can be plain words or regular expressions, and many options change what counts as a match and what is printed.
when: Find a flag, password or username inside a log, dump, memory image or whole folder.
Count or list evidence: failed logins, an IP, a path, a user agent.
Filter the output of another command (cmd | grep word).

examples.title: Why -F matters
examples.cmd: printf 'flag{1x3}\nflag{1.3}\n' > t.txt; echo '--- regex:'; grep 'flag{1.3}' t.txt; echo '--- fixed string:'; grep -F 'flag{1.3}' t.txt

examples.title: Whole words only  (-w)

examples.title: Just the exit status  (-q)
examples.cmd: grep -q admin access.log && echo found admin

options.plain: Treat the pattern as an extended regular expression, where + ? | ( ) work without backslashes.

options.plain: Treat the pattern as plain text, not a regular expression.

options.plain: Treat the pattern as a basic regular expression. This is the default.
options.use: You want to be explicit, or undo an earlier -E.

options.plain: Treat the pattern as a Perl-style regular expression (lookahead, \d).
options.use: Complex patterns that -E cannot express; not available in every grep.

options.plain: Give the pattern with an option, so you can use several -e and patterns that start with a dash.
options.use: Searching for more than one thing, or for -x.

options.plain: Read the patterns from a file, one per line.
options.use: A long list of indicators (bad IPs, keywords).

options.plain: Ignore upper and lower case.

options.plain: Turn off an earlier -i (for example from an alias).

options.plain: Show lines that do NOT match.
options.use: Remove the noise to see what is left.

options.plain: Match whole words only.
options.use: root should not match rootkit.

options.plain: Match only when the whole line matches.
options.use: Exact-line checks, such as a specific entry in a list.

options.plain: Print the number of matching lines instead of the lines.
options.use: How many failures? how many hits?

options.plain: Highlight the matches in colour (WHEN is always, never or auto).
options.use: Reading results on a terminal; use always when piping into less -R.

options.plain: List only the names of files that contain no match.
options.use: Which files lack a required line?

options.plain: List only the names of files that contain a match.
options.use: Which files mention this? Fast triage of a folder.

options.plain: Stop after NUM matching lines.
options.use: Huge files where the first hit is enough.

options.plain: Print only the matched part of the line.
options.use: Pull out IPs, e-mails, flags.

options.plain: Print nothing; just set the exit status (0 found, 1 not found).
options.use: Inside if statements and scripts.

options.plain: Hide error messages about files that do not exist or cannot be read.
options.use: Recursive searches full of permission errors.

options.plain: Print the byte position of each match (with -o, of the match itself).
options.use: Locating data in a binary so you can open it with xxd -s.

options.plain: Always print the file name in front of each line.
options.use: Searching one file but wanting the name in the output.

options.plain: Never print file names, even for several files.
options.use: You only want the lines.

options.plain: Use LABEL as the file name when reading from standard input.
options.use: Piped input should show a name.

options.plain: Prefix each line with its line number.
options.use: You need to open the file at that spot later.

options.plain: Align the prefixes (file name, line number) with a tab.
options.use: Neat columns of output.

options.plain: End file names with a NUL byte instead of a newline (with -l, -L or -H).
options.use: Safe piping to xargs -0 when names contain spaces.

options.plain: Also print NUM lines after each match.
options.use: Read what happened right after the hit.

options.plain: Also print NUM lines before each match.
options.use: Read what led to the hit.

options.plain: Also print NUM lines before and after each match.
options.use: Read the surroundings of a hit.

options.plain: Use SEP instead of -- between groups of context lines.
options.use: Making context output easier to parse.

options.plain: Do not print a separator between groups of context lines.
options.use: Clean output for further processing.

options.plain: Treat a binary file as if it were text.
options.use: Searching images, binaries and memory dumps.

options.plain: Say how binary files are handled: binary (default message), text, or without-match.
options.use: Control the Binary file matches message.

options.plain: Skip binary files as if they had no matches.
options.use: Searching source trees without noise from compiled files.

options.plain: Do not strip carriage returns; read files as raw bytes (matters on Windows).

options.plain: Treat input as lines ended by NUL bytes instead of newlines.

options.plain: Say what to do with devices and sockets: read or skip.

options.plain: Say what to do with directories: read, skip or recurse.

options.plain: Search every file under a folder, not following symbolic links.
options.use: Search a whole project or extracted archive.

options.plain: Like -r, but follow symbolic links.

options.plain: Only search files whose names match GLOB.
options.use: Limit a recursive search to *.py or *.log.

options.plain: Skip files whose names match GLOB.
options.use: Ignore minified or binary files.

options.plain: Skip files that match any pattern listed in FILE.
options.use: A long ignore list.

options.plain: Skip directories whose names match GLOB.
options.use: Ignore .git or node_modules.

options.plain: Flush output after every line.
options.use: Watching a live log: tail -f log | grep --line-buffered x.

options.plain: Print the version and exit.

options.plain: Print a short usage message and exit.
options.use: A quick reminder without opening the manual.

mistakes: Quote the pattern: unquoted * and $ are expanded by the shell before grep sees them.
grep pattern * skips hidden files: use -r on the folder.
A dot in a regular expression means any character: escape it (\.) or use -F for an IP such as 10.0.0.5.
On binary files without -a, grep prints only Binary file matches.
-P is not in every grep (macOS, BusyBox): -E is the portable choice.
